body.prompt: A cramped but cozy Korean apartment kitchen at 2 a.m., lit only by one warm pendant lamp hanging over a low wooden folding table; the rest of the room sinks into soft blue night shadow. Through the window behind, the lit windows of tall Seoul apartment towers glow in the dark. On the counter: an electric rice cooker with a tiny red light and a wisp of steam, a squat kimchi refrigerator, red rubber dish gloves draped over the edge of the sink, a stack of stainless-steel rice bowls. A Korean mother in her late fifties with short curly permed black hair, reading glasses pushed up on her head, wearing a pastel floral apron over a lilac cardigan, kneels on a woven straw mat on the floor beside a big open plain brown cardboard box. With both hands she carefully lowers a glass jar of bright red napa-cabbage kimchi, wrapped twice in clear plastic bags, into the box. Already packed tightly inside: stacked clear plastic containers of side dishes (seasoned spinach, glossy braised black beans, tiny stir-fried anchovies), a bundle of plain red instant-noodle packs, sheets of dark dried seaweed, a mesh bag of orange persimmons. Her face is tired but deeply tender, a quiet gentle smile. The magpie sits on the corner of the low table holding a roll of brown packing tape in its wings, watching her with soft shiny eyes.
